papers.title_in_file: SCOOP: A Quantum-Computing Framework for Constrained Combinatorial Optimization
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, I Introduction, II Related work, IV (MINDS derivation, Theorem 1), VII-VIII evaluation text, IX Conclusions; Sections V-VI and appendix derivations skimmed only
papers.what_it_is: A QAOA framework that turns a constrained combinatorial problem into an unconstrained twin, then post-processes classically.

assertions.value: The authors state that SCOOP derives an unconstrained problem from a constrained one, giving a penalty-free cost Hamiltonian for QAOA, with classical post-processing of the QAOA solutions.
quotes: Our framework guides the derivation of an unconstrained COP from the constrained COP. This process results in a penalty-free cost Hamiltonian that is well-suited for QAOA.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' description of their own framework, supported by derivations and simulations in the paper.

assertions.value: The paper states that Theorem 1 shows MINDS and MAXPD are SCOOP twins, so an optimal MAXPD solution yields a minimum dominating set through Algorithm 1.
quotes: Theorem 1 below concludes the proof that MINDS and MAXPD are SCOOP twins.
Theorem 1 implies that, given an optimal solution to MAXPD PD for a graph G, we can obtain a minimum dominating set for G using Algorithm 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1, Sec. IV.

assertions.value: The authors report that the experiments ran on Xanadu's PennyLane simulator on 3-regular graphs with up to ten qubits and eight layers of QAOA; they state that execution on IBM hardware is future work.
assertions.anchor: Sec. IX Conclusions and Future Work
quotes: These experiments were conducted using Xanadu's PennyLane simulator on 3-regular graphs with up to ten qubits and eight layers of QAOA.
Furthermore, we intend to execute both QUBO and HUBO formulations of the unconstrained SCOOP twins on IBM's quantum hardware.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. IX states the evaluation scope.
assertions.reader_inference: No hardware run and no instance beyond ten qubits is reported.

assertions.value: The authors report over 60% probability of sampling near-optimal solutions at p = 1 on their small simulated graphs.
quotes: Our approach yields over 60% probability of sampling nearoptimal solutions at p = 1
assertions.certainty_reason: One simulated study on small graphs.

papers.title_in_file: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning for Multiclass Image Classification
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, I Introduction, VI results text and Table IV discussion, VII Conclusion; circuit sections III-V skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A QCNN variant that reuses measurements of qubits discarded at pooling, fed to classical heads, tested on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and OrganAMNIST.

assertions.value: The authors report that adding discarded-qubit measurements raised test accuracy from 68.51% to 93.55% on MNIST, from 81.40% to 96.45% on Fashion-MNIST and from 69.13% to 88.50% on OrganAMNIST, against a baseline with all other settings identical.
quotes: test accuracy climbed from 68.51% to 93.55% on MNIST, from 81.40% to 96.45% on Fashion-MNIST, and from 69.13% to 88.50% on OrganAMNIST
assertions.certainty_reason: One study; the baseline omits the recycled branch. The paper's own runs.
assertions.reader_inference: The gains are large partly because the baseline is weak; the comparison is against the authors' own ablation.

assertions.value: The authors state that their model achieves the highest reported accuracies against recent quantum and hybrid baselines while keeping a 262-parameter footprint.
quotes: our model achieves the highest reported accuracies while keeping a compact 262-parameter footprint.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' comparison with two chosen baselines.

assertions.value: The authors state that they evaluate on classical image datasets, and that intrinsically quantum problems such as topological-phase recognition or error syndrome classification remain future work.
quotes: Although our benchmarks focus on classical image data, the hybrid QCNN is independent of how the input state is prepared.
Extending the evaluation to intrinsically quantum problems, such as topological-phase recognition or error syndrome classification, remains a natural direction for future work.
assertions.certainty_reason: Introduction states the scope of the evaluation.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Annealing Enhanced Markov-Chain Monte Carlo
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Results (spectral gap, energy convergence), Discussion and Conclusion; Methods details skimmed
papers.what_it_is: QAEMCMC uses quantum annealing to generate MCMC proposal states; benchmarked by simulation on the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model.

assertions.value: The authors report that the quantum annealing update gives a larger spectral gap than the classical updates, and that more than doubled quantum enhancement exists in the fitted exponents.
quotes: More than doubled quantum enhancement exists for the exponents.
We exhibited that QAEMCMC yielded a larger spectral gap than the classical updates.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation of small SK instances.

assertions.value: The authors report that the QA update gives a better estimator at least about twelve times faster than the classical updates in the averaged-energy benchmark.
quotes: The QA update gives a better estimator, at least more than about twelve times faster than the classical updates.
assertions.certainty_reason: One simulated benchmark, averaged over independent MCMC runs.

assertions.value: The authors state that their simulation was limited to small system size and that whether QAEMCMC is effective for large-size problems is an open question.
quotes: Our simulation was limited to the small system size, and whether QAEMCMC is effective for large-size problems is an open question.
assertions.certainty_reason: Discussion and Conclusion, p.7.

papers.title_in_file: Gaussian Process Model Kernels for Noisy Optimization in Variational Quantum Algorithms
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Sec. 2 results text on GPM fits and RotoGP, Sec. 4 Conclusions; kernel derivations and appendices skimmed
papers.what_it_is: Trigonometric kernels for Gaussian process models of VQA cost functions, and RotoGP, a GPM-equipped line-search optimizer, tested in simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that trigonometric kernels generally require fewer data points to reach a given precision of the GPM-predicted minimum than other kernels, on LiH ground state and unweighted MaxCut problems.
quotes: trigonometric kernels generally require fewer data points to reach a given precision compared to other kernels.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated benchmarks on two problem types.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the RotoGP optimization the trigonometric kernels gave both higher accuracy and faster convergence than bare RotoSolve.
quotes: In both cases, the trigonometric kernels improve upon the performance of the bare RotoSolve without GPM: we find both higher accuracy and faster convergence.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated optimization runs.

assertions.value: The authors state that the relative gains of trigonometric kernels appear problem-dependent, and that in one panel (Fig. 2(f)) the non-stationary trigonometric kernel performs worse than all the other kernels.
quotes: Additionally, the relative gains of trigonometric kernels appear problem-dependent.
An exception to this conclusion is Fig. 2(f), where the non-stationary trigonometric kernel is performing worse than all the other ones
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. 4 and Sec. 2.2 state the limits.

papers.title_in_file: Effect of barren plateaus on gradient-free optimization
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, 1 Introduction, 3 Results (Proposition 1, Corollary 1, numerics), Discussion; appendix proof not checked line by line
papers.what_it_is: Shows analytically and numerically that gradient-free optimizers are also hindered by barren plateaus.

assertions.value: The paper proves that cost function differences, which gradient-free optimizers use to make decisions, are exponentially suppressed in a barren plateau.
quotes: Our main result proves that cost function differences, which are the basis for making decisions in a gradient-free optimization, are exponentially suppressed in a barren plateau.
assertions.certainty_reason: Proposition 1, Sec. 3.1.

assertions.value: The authors report that, training a parameterized quantum circuit in a barren plateau with Nelder-Mead, Powell and COBYLA, the number of shots required grows exponentially with the number of qubits.
quotes: show that the number of shots required in the optimization grows exponentially with the number of qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical runs for three optimizers.

assertions.value: The authors state that their results cast doubt on the notion that the choice of optimizer could avoid barren plateaus, and that Proposition 1 applies to optimizers such as Nelder-Mead that compare points.
quotes: Our work casts doubt on the notion that the choice of optimizer could provide a strategy to avoid barren plateaus.
Proposition 1 is relevant to gradient-free optimizers that search through the landscape starting from a (random) initial point.
assertions.certainty_reason: Discussion states what the results cover.

papers.title_in_file: Balanced k-Means Clustering on an Adiabatic Quantum Computer
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, I Introduction, IV experiments text (run time, Iris), V Conclusion; QUBO derivation skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A QUBO formulation of balanced k-means clustering run on a D-Wave 2000Q, compared with classical k-means.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum approach partitions data with similar accuracy to the classical approaches, even when running on imperfect hardware.
quotes: We demonstrated that our quantum approach partitions data with similar accuracy to the classical approaches, even when running on imperfect hardware.
assertions.certainty_reason: Small problems on a D-Wave 2000Q, Iris subsets.

assertions.value: The authors report that the quantum approach performed slower than both classical algorithms in each case, and that the quantum run time was dominated by embedding time.
quotes: In each case, the quantum approach performed slower than both classical algorithms. However, the quantum run time was dominated by the embedding time.
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured run times on small problems.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's scalability claim rests on extrapolation to future hardware, not on a measured speedup.

assertions.value: The authors state that, owing to qubit limits of the hardware, problems that need more than 64 binary variables are impossible on the D-Wave 2000Q, and the entire Iris data set could not be clustered.
quotes: problems that require more than 64 binary variables (N k > 64) are impossible on the D-Wave 2000Q
Unfortunately, due to qubit limitations on modern hardware, it is impossible to perform quantum balanced k-means clustering on the entire data set.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. IV states the hardware limit.

papers.title_in_file: Fourier series weight in quantum machine learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, I Introduction, IV.E Limitations, VII-VIII results discussion, IX Conclusion; Sec. VI derivation skimmed
papers.what_it_is: Variational quantum models viewed as Fourier series, tested in PennyLane on interpolation, classification and signal processing.

assertions.value: The authors state that their results conclude that one can strongly consider the quantum computer a Fourier series.
quotes: The results conclude that we can strongly consider the quantum computer a Fourier series.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' conclusion, building on earlier Fourier-series work they cite.
assertions.reader_inference: This restates prior Fourier-series work on quantum models more than it adds a new result.

assertions.value: The authors report some classifiers with accuracy greater than 92%, for example 92.5% on a two-circle task and 92.2% on a square task.
quotes: we are talking about 92.5% accuracy
an accuracy of 92.2%
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated toy classification in PennyLane.

assertions.value: The authors state that the model has limits for the highest-frequency input signals, and that hardware qubit scarcity and error cap the model size.
quotes: we have also detected some limitations in better adapting the model to the highest-frequency input signals.
The qubits' scarcity and susceptibility to errors and decoherence significantly cap the complexity and size of the models we can reliably implement.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. IV.E and Sec. IX.

papers.title_in_file: The Grand Challenge of Quantum Applications
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, five-stage overview, Stage III discussion, Conclusion; Stage IV and early-fault-tolerant compilation sections skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A Google Quantum AI perspective proposing a five-stage framework for developing useful quantum applications.

assertions.value: The authors propose a five-stage framework for quantum applications research, from algorithm discovery to application deployment.
quotes: We divide that quest into five stages:
assertions.certainty_reason: A perspective's own framework, no experiment.

assertions.value: The authors argue that identifying concrete problem instances with quantum advantage (Stage II) and matching these to real-world applications (Stage III) are the most significant hurdles.
quotes: the challenges of identifying concrete problem instances with quantum advantage (Stage II) and matching these problems to real-world applications (Stage III) represent the most significant hurdles to expanding the landscape of quantum applications.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' argued position.

assertions.value: The authors state that, outside of quantum simulation and cryptanalysis, connecting abstract algorithms to real-world problems has proven difficult to demonstrate.
quotes: Outside of quantum simulation and cryptanalysis, this connection has proven difficult to demonstrate.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' view of the field, from Google Quantum AI.
assertions.reader_inference: The team is vendor-affiliated, but this is a statement about the field and not a product claim.
